utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before you're invited, Mr. Re, to call your next witness, there was an issue that still needs to be resolved because the Appeals Chamber has given a decision on lifting of protective measures, but there is a condition to that decision, the condition being that VWS should notify the registry and the parties of the outcome of their conversations with the witness about lifting the protective measures. And as far as the Chamber was aware, such notification had not officially taken place, so therefore the Trial Chamber would very much like to hear from VWS at this moment what the results were, and since informally the Trial Chamber learned that the outcome was such that the protective measures could be lifted, there's no need to go into private session. We invited Ms. Wintgen to inform, to notify the parties and the registry and of course the Chamber about the outcome of the conversations with the witness. Could you please inform the Chamber, Ms. Wintgen?

utterances.speaker: MS. WINTGEN
utterances.text: I met with the witness after his arrival here last week and he not only confirmed that he wants to have the protective measures lifted; he's verbally asked for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Ms. Wintgen. This means that now all conditions are met for the lifting of confidential -- of protective measures in relation to your next witness, which is Mr. Kabashi, if I understand -- if we understand the -- yes. I have some difficulties. My line of sight with Mr. Re is not perfect, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Ms. Issa is taking the witness, so

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Ms. Issa will be taking the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- so maybe Your Honour doesn't need to see me as much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Wintgen, I thank you very much. I take it that this informal notification which is now on the record is sufficient. Yes. Then I'd like to thank you very much for coming to the courtroom, Ms. Wintgen, and you are excused.

utterances.speaker: MS. WINTGEN
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, if you want to raise a procedural issue, I would like to raise another procedural issue first --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so you'll get an opportunity. Judge Hoepfel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to make a statement which concerns myself and a certain member of the Prosecution team, Ms. Romana Schweiger. Ms. Schweiger happens not only to be from my country, Austria, but was also my student and my assistant at the University of Vienna. As you are aware, Ms. Schweiger was placed on the Prosecution team in this case after the trial had already begun. I have known Ms. Schweiger for a number of years, first as an undergraduate student and later as doctoral student. I was her senior doctoral supervisor. After her doctorate in March 2004, Ms. Schweiger became on basis of her excellent results in international criminal law, assistant of the University of Vienna in the department of criminal law and criminology. Since that time and until I started my work here as a Judge in December 2005, she was a member of my research team. We published two short joint articles in the German "Jahrbuch fur Menschen," that is, the yearbook of human rights. Our cooperation ceased from the moment she became a member of the OTP. The Trial Chamber is, as I can say after consultation with my colleagues, certain that the former academic relationship between Ms. Schweiger and myself would not in any way influence my opinion on any matter in the performance of my judicial duties in this trial. I am and remain impartial. Although what I said is essentially in the public domain, I thought that it would be good to place it on the record in order to provide full transparency to the parties and the public about my former academic relationship with Ms. Schweiger. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, you would like to raise something.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. There's a matter I wanted to raise, if I may. Simply this: The Trial Chamber should have been provided in respect of the next witness with a 92 ter statement and a consolidated witness statement. The consolidated witness statement differs in some respects from earlier witness statements made by this witness, and in particular certain incidents referred to or recorded in earlier witness statements are not included within the consolidated witness statement. And I have sought clarification over the previous days of the Prosecution's intention in respect of those matters which have been deliberately omitted from the consolidated witness statement. Until this morning, it was my understanding that the Prosecution's intention was to lead in chief evidence only which was contained within the consolidated witness statement, but in preparing for this witness I noticed that at least one incident that is referred to in the earlier statements but is not included within the consolidated witness statement is nonetheless included within those passages in the Limaj transcript which the Prosecution have identified in response to the Trial Chamber's invitation as being of potential relevance. There's obviously a tension between the stated position as I understood it to be until this morning and the indications that the Prosecution had given in relation to the Limaj transcript. Having had an opportunity to discuss the position with Ms. Issa this morning, I'll allow her, if I may, to outline the Prosecution's approach. But it may well be that, for example, in respect of one particular incident I have in mind that the Prosecution's decision omit it from the consolidated witness statement was made, as I am informed, on the basis that the incident took place outside of the indictment period and was therefore irrelevant. And so the question in my mind was and I've put it to the Prosecution this morning, if it's irrelevant because it's outside the indictment period for the purposes of the consolidated witness statement, how is it relevant notwithstanding that it is outside the indictment period for the purposes of the Limaj transcript. What we have provisionally agreed and subject to the Trial Chamber's view, is that as and when any issue of that kind arises or indeed other issues that are referred to in the consolidated witness statement that fall outside the indictment period, as and when the Prosecution moves to begin to elicit such material, and Ms. Issa is on notice of which passages in particular fall into that category, she will notify the Trial Chamber and the Defence and the relevance of the passage can be argued as and when it arises, rather than taking stock at the outset of the witness's evidence of each passage and inviting a ruling in advance. If that course commends itself to the Trial Chamber, we thought you ought to be on notice of what's been provisionally agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that is in respect to all three accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's understood. The Chamber accepts the proposed course to be taken, so therefore all counsel are expected to raise the issue when it comes up.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And in terms of practical handling of this witness and timetables, I've had an opportunity to canvass with all parties including the Prosecution very rough estimated timings and I think the collective view from both sides of the bar, indeed all sides of the bar is that it is likely that this witness will take the whole of today and the whole of Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the whole of Wednesday --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thursday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- will not be much --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because we are not sitting on Wednesday but I take it --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In other words, the testimony of this witness is likely to occupy two full days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two full days. Okay. It's good to be informed about that. Then, Ms. Issa, are you ready to call your next witness which then will be Mr. Kabashi?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour. Good morning, I just -- just at the outset I just wanted as a matter of clarification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just very simple. It takes us some time to get Mr. Kabashi here. Do you think you could address us on the matter in one or two minutes because then I'll already ask Madam Usher to go and look for the witness. Well, he's nearby. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. It won't take long. I just wanted to clarify something that Mr. Emmerson just pointed out, which is, although I'm not strictly leading evidence from the original statement, as I indicated to Mr. Emmerson, obviously the 92 ter transcript, the Limaj transcript, is before the Chamber and it's -- we anticipate will be evidence, therefore, before the Chamber. And so therefore, anything that's relevant, we pointed out which portions are relevant within the 92 ter transcript may be of, we would submit, of relevance to the Chamber, and just because something's outside of the indictment period does not necessarily mean that it is irrelevant. And so I just wanted to clarify that, just because it's not in the consolidated statement, it's still in the transcript which is considered to be -- which we seek to put before the Chamber as evidence pursuant to the Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. You are aware that the Chamber expressed some concerns about the relevance and whether or not we'll admit the whole of it or whether we would exclude certain portions is still to be considered. We have not decided on the matter yet, and that needs more detailed review of the material.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I think Ms. Issa will be aware that the Trial Chamber has already indicated in respect of matters that go to central or important aspects of the evidence, that oral testimony will be required rather than simply the reliance on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Not to say that it's not evidence, but the Chamber would like to hear that evidence, perhaps details and perhaps not necessarily everything to be repeated, but not to say here the accused is -- according to the testimony, has beaten a person and then not to say any word about that. That's not the way the Chamber expects the parties to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And in one sense in respect to the issues that we've been discussing in relation to this witness's testimony, that point comes into sharp focus since there will be passages of the transcript the admission of which remains an issue in contention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Troop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just raise a technical matter, which is my client is currently not in receipt of translation. So perhaps we could pause briefly whilst that problem is resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that -- are we on the right channel, Madam Usher? The accused ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be a technical problem which cannot be resolved by just pushing some buttons. Sometimes it helps if you take another socket.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I think the indication is that the problem's been resolved. Perhaps you could just clarify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I now am looking at you, Mr. Brahimaj, Mr. Balaj, and Mr. Haradinaj, and I see you all three -- from your body language, I understand you all three receive the translation in your own language. Thank you. Then we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is brought in, I just briefly want to raise something about the next witness - it's fine - and that is we indicated I think on Thursday that we would have another witness later in the week. We've subsequently received notification last night that there is a difficulty with the witness coming this week, so it may be that this witness is the only one we have here this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, since we are -- since we need the full two days still available, as I understand, that should cause no major problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Can you hear me in a language you understand, Mr. Kabashi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this declaration is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I declare solemnly that I will say the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kabashi. Please be seated. Mr. Kabashi, you'll now be examined by Ms. Issa who's counsel for the Prosecution, and you will see her to your right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Honourable Judge, can I make a small clarification before such questions are started?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, tell me what kind of clarification you would like to make.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In connection with my position as a witness and my arrival here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I can inform you that where you earlier have testified before this Tribunal with protective measures, as the Chamber understands, upon your specific wish the protective measures have been lifted now. That's just for you to know; that's why you are testifying in public. Would you like to say anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, just I would like to say something about my position and my coming here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if -- since I do not know what it is, please tell me briefly what you would like to address.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not take much of your time. I gave my statement a long time ago. I have also accepted to give my statement in order to throw light on the crimes and to prevent the crimes which are still going on in Kosovo today. However, since then I am threatened by the Prosecutors to come here and give my witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, to the extent that you were told that you have to appear if called as a witness, then that is correct. You have a civil duty. I'm not going at this moment to discuss. If there's something more, then of course matters might be different and then the Chamber would like to know about it. But I don't know whether we should do that immediately in public session, because we do not know what will come, and therefore it's easier to lift confidentiality at a later stage than to make any mistake in this respect. Mr. Re, I think it would be your primary concern, although Mr. Emmerson is standing. Any suggestion as to how to -- first of all, are you aware -- were you prepared that such a statement would be made by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Absolutely not. We had no idea --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- what the witness is saying or why he would walk into the courtroom and say this before he starts his testimony. There's certainly no indication in any of his statements which he's signed and are in his own language of anything of that nature The Prosecution of course is very concerned about any such allegation. We don't know who he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: However, the Prosecution is also very concerned of public perceptions, and if there are any allegations that are dealt with in closed session, a perception may well be given to the public at large that something is being hidden --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- which should not be hidden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, what then would be your conclusion, to proceed in open session or -- I mean, the problem is that I can't foresee what the witness is going to say. Therefore, I know for sure that if something is -- has become public which should not have become public, then it's very difficult to have full damage control, whereas the other way around, it's easier, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I would be content with doing it the other way around initially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Initially. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, provided the matter is explored before the witness begins to testify, I am neutral as to whether it is done in closed or open session, but I entirely see the wisdom of the course that Your Honour recommends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think private session would do, Mr. Re. It's just -- it's not the face of the witness, it's not anything else, it's just what he says. So therefore, we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, the Chamber has heard submissions by the parties made on the basis of what you told us before. We'll pay further attention what you said. The Chamber will seek more information about it, but what you just told us is not an obstacle to start your examination as a witness. And I'd like to make perfectly clear to you that whatever you know when examined, you should tell us about what you know. If there's anything you would be disappointed about that you couldn't talk about it, then at the end of your testimony we always could consider whether there are any subjects which you draw our attention to and which the Chamber then would find relevant to see whether any further testimony should be elicited from you on those subjects you consider important. But we start at this moment with your examination on the basis of what the parties would like to ask you, and you are under an obligation to answer the questions in accordance with the solemn declaration you gave; that is, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Ms. Issa, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't know if we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kabashi. I just -- could you please -- as I understand it, your full name is Shefqet Kabashi. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And can you tell us when your date of birth is?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: 1st of July, 1976.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And as I understand it, sir, you were born in the village of Zahaq. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And what municipality is that in?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Peje municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And you are a Kosovar Albanian. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And without saying where you work specifically, sir, could you tell us what your present occupation is?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I'm a manager of a small pizzeria, a small restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And prior to that where did you work?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: In construction before I went to the states, and then in the Kosova police service as a security officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, approximately two weeks ago on -- precisely on the 10th and 12th and 14th of May, 2007, you provided a statement to the Prosecution. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And I understand, sir, that you speak pretty good English, but you've reviewed that statement in your mother tongue for accuracy, haven't you, in Albanian?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I was given this statement for a read-back on Friday in the afternoon, when I just flew back from the United States of America, and I did not pay much attention, I was not in a state to pay that much attention to the read-back. But the purpose was for me to come here and explain to the Judges that there are no conditions for witnesses to come here and testify. That's why I, again, would like to call on the Trial Chamber to alleviate me from giving a statement because I'm not in a position to give evidence. I have many explanations, facts to explain. The Judge interrupted me, didn't allow me to explain, but I would like to explain those facts because I'm the one who lives in Kosova. I'm the one who has gone through a lot during the war, and I am the one who is brought here to tell the truth about things that I saw, heard from somebody else, or that I personally experienced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, the Chamber is not expecting to you -- you to do anything else than what you just told us what you're brought here for; that is, to tell us the truth about the things that you saw or you heard or that you personally experienced. That's your civil duty, and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, I do not fully understand what you would like to explain because you could wait and listen what questions will be put to you, and then to answer those questions in accordance with what you did see, what you did hear, and what you did experience.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, it is true that it is our duty, but within the framework of a normal life. Since this normal life does not exist in the state where I live, where people get killed and to -- nowadays the reasons why they got killed are not known, when lives of people have changed, I don't know in what conditions I can give a statement here. I cannot accommodate myself to giving this statement here because of the things I went through. If we want to hear about the truth about the things that happened in Kosova, let alone Yugoslavia as a whole, my statement is not at all regular, not to 1 per cent of it. It has been worked on and only the interests of the Prosecutors have been represented there. And that's why I explained that I signed that statement because of the threats and because of my will to come here and tell you that there are no normal conditions for a witness to come here and testify. That's why I appeal to you on my behalf and on behalf of many of my friends to allow us not to give statement because I really don't know in what other words to explain. If a person doesn't live in normal life conditions, I don't know how that person can come here and give evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your observations are still puzzling me, Mr. Kabashi, because in this court you can give the answers you consider to be the right answers. Therefore, if anything has happened in the past, then we would like to hear from you what the answers should be. That's exactly the reason why you are here, that we don't have read on paper what you may have said at other occasions, but that we hear your answers to the questions put to you. At the same time, in your observations there seems to be some elements of fear for the future caused by whomever, and of course it is then surprising that you, as we understood, have fully consented in lifting whatever protective measures there may have been in the past. So therefore --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but it's not a matter of fear. I am disappointed, and not only disappointed, but certain things that should not happen and should not be done in modern world have happened. You, yourself, may not have come across such things, but there were persons who were asked questions as witnesses and whose names don't even appear on witness lists because they have been killed. I don't want protective measures because such measures do not exist in reality; they only exist within the boundaries of this courtroom, not outside it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, we will have a break now. After the break, you will be examined. You are under a duty to answer all the questions, and if there's anything in your statement which is not in accordance with what the truthful answer to the questions would be, just give us the truthful answers, nothing else. That's what we are going to do after the break, and then the Chamber wishes not to continue long debates on problems that may be there but that are best resolved by answering questions, first questions that will be put to you by the Office of the Prosecution, counsel for the Prosecution; after that, questions that will be put to you by Defence counsel; and perhaps some questions as well put by the Chamber. We'll resume at 11.00 and then continue the examination-in-chief of Mr. Kabashi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Issa, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, before the break we were talking about your statement. Now, before the 1st of June when you said you came in and reviewed your statement, was the statement sent to you before that time?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. I have also another request for the Judges, if I am allowed to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we can continue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it depends on what the question would be. As I said before, we don't want to enter into a continued debate on all kind of things. If, however, you would prefer to give your testimony, now with protective measures, you can apply for that. That would -- one of the options to be considered would be, for example, closed session. If that's the kind of request you would like to make, please do so. Also keep in mind, Mr. Kabashi, that we are not going to fill the next two days by discussing all kind of matters. The Chamber would like to hear your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not requesting protective measures. As I told you earlier, I do not need them; however, I'm not in a position to give my testimony. I'm not here capable to give this testimony psychologically and morally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, you are under a duty to give that testimony. The Chamber cannot understand what moral reasons there could be not to truthfully answer any questions to you. Therefore, you are urged to carefully listen to the questions and to answer them. Ms. Issa, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, I agree to give my testimony but I'm not capable of doing it. I'm not in a position to do that. I'm not capable to do that for different, many reasons. If you want to listen to these reasons, I could tell you, but please do not push me any further. I cannot talk about the things you are asking me after so many things that have happened. If you want to force me, to take me to prison, I will go to prison. Sometimes they keep you in prison even if you are not a criminal. I have been kept in prison before, even though I've not been guilty. So this is my final request. I am not capable of responding the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, the Chamber will give you an opportunity to explain the reasons. The Chamber would like to know whether you would like to do that in open session or in private session. The Chamber immediately adds to this that the Chamber will make its determinations on -- on the basis of what you and perhaps the parties will submit to the Chamber. Therefore, you should not misunderstand our decision. The fact that we are giving you an opportunity to explain the reasons does not automatically mean that we accept those reasons, and therefore it's only after we've heard you and if there's any need to have heard the parties, we'll then determine whether or not the Chamber will grant your request. So therefore, first please give us the reasons and tell us whether you would like to give them in private session or in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said earlier, I do not need closed session. Everything could be in open session; however, if you want to listen to what I said earlier, in view of what has happened in my life during the war, with the events after the war, and with the investigators of the Prosecutors, with things that have happened with the investigations in Kosova, I'm not pleased with what has happened and I'm not able to testify. I cannot, very briefly, I cannot, not because somebody forces me, not because I'm afraid of anybody. If you, as Judges, compel me to do that, I can tell you that I'm not able. You can take your decision, but I'm asking you and asking the Prosecutors to release me, to allow me to go back to Kosova to see my children. If you want to send me to prison, there is nothing I can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, on the basis of what you've said, it might be difficult to conclude that it's anything more that you don't want to testify. You said: "I cannot." You're not afraid. You say, don't compel me; I just can't do it, which sounds to some extent as, I'm not willing to do it. Could you give us any specific reasons why you can't, as you said. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to rise because I know this is a delicate process and one doesn't want, especially with a witness who can speak some English and therefore can't easily be resolved by the removal of headphones, one doesn't want the witness to be backwards and forwards. Obviously, there may be explanations of the witness's unwillingness to testify. I don't want to say anything in front of the witness that may prompt a suggestion. I don't know how Your Honour wants to deal with it, but my slight concern rather crosses over a concern that was raised with another witness, which is that if in effect he's being invited to give answers to questions that could result in him being in a position where he's putting himself in contempt, then at some point before he does so he ought either to be advised or be cautioned. And if not, then some exploration from him of what the possible alternative reasons may be. I'm sorry, I'm trying to be helpful, but I don't know if that is helpful or not. I'm in Your Honour's hands. I'm being cryptic, I suppose, about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the reason why I'm re-reading what you said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm trying not to be suggestive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm re-reading what you -- yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If the Chamber understands what Mr. Emmerson is saying, that would be fine. Perhaps I can help in the code. You do recall that the other day I was on my feet quite a bit with regard to another witness and I was making a particular kind of point in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To say that everything is now clear to me, let me just --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let me take the bull by the horns. The witness has already given some answers, which tend to suggest that in his view some of the assertions in the statements that he's made do not properly represent the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, you mean to remind him of --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, there are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- all sorts of possible permutations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That arise, as a matter of fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Given that he's already testified, there are all possible permutations why a witness might at this stage not wish to testify again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I could perhaps explain that to the witness. If, Mr. Kabashi, if one of your concerns would be - I'm not saying it is, because there are a lot of potential explanations for the present situation, and you're finally the only one who knows at this moment which is the true explanation - if you would be concerned that by testifying at this moment you would deviate from answers you've given earlier, both under oath and in statements taken by investigators, and that it would cause you problems in now giving testimony in deviation of what you said earlier, if that would be among your concerns, then please tell us so that we can see whether any solution can be found for that. It needs an interpretation of our Rules on this matter, which excludes Prosecution for one offence if a witness is forced to give answers. But I would then discuss that with the parties at a later stage. But could you please first inform us whether that is among your concerns.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I heard here Mr. Emmerson said the same thing, whether I'm not quite sure that I will say the same thing I said earlier. I'm sure that what I've said is correct and accurate. I could give you further details about that. However, I told you that following what has happened during the investigations and after the events in my country, after the event that occurred to me personally following the recent threats, and at present my personal situation. So in view of all these things, I cannot give testimony. It's not because I'm afraid of anybody, it's not because that I will not say the same thing I have said in the statement. I apologise, but I cannot give you testimony here. Many injustices have occurred, many things have happened and I'm sick of them. Many things have occurred during the investigations in Kosova, the way they handled people there. In my opinion, that was something which should not have happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, it's of no use to refer in general terms to injustices done during investigations. If there's any specific point where you consider that injustice has been done to you which caused you or contributed to your determination at this moment not to testify, please tell us about it, but general allegations are of no use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if there's any injustice done to you you would like to refer to, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned what I wanted to say earlier. I told you there have been many injustice. Everything that was done was not just. The investigations, but what has happened to me earlier were not proper. They didn't ask me, indeed, questions about what has really happened to me. I think the way things were done was not just, and the same thing should be said so about the way other people were questioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, I earlier offered you that if there would be anything you considered important enough for us to know and that you would be given an opportunity to now tell us what you, as I understand, wanted to tell earlier but no questions were put to you in this respect, so such an opportunity will be given to you at the end of your testimony. Therefore, I do not understand. You're complaining about behaviour which doesn't meet what you would deem to be proper. It's now offered to you, that is, you answer the questions in full accordance with the truth. If there's anything you consider important not asked, you can tell us at the end of your testimony and we could see whether we could give you an opportunity to add something to your testimony. At the same time, even if you would say, Let me first tell you what happened to me personally, because that seems to contribute to your hesitation to testify, we could give you an opportunity to do that, but not instead of but in addition to answering questions put to you by the parties and by the Chamber. So if you would like to address us on what happened to you, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was not the problem, sir. We talked about other things. The problem is that I belong to that country. Since people come there and investigate and they do not look, indeed, at the true cases, but they bring people here simply to get some evidence in order to have their wages increased and to -- in this way they do damage to our country. So for me to come here under such circumstance is not correct and I cannot accept it and I cannot give testimony under these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, whatever went wrong in the past, whatever people did in order to get better wages, this is the moment to correct that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not understand what you want me to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I want you to say is that where you allude to improper behaviour by investigators who did not care about the truth but just wanted to provide some evidence in order to get better living conditions, that if that was the case, then forget about what happened and now do it as it should be done; that is, to give the information in full accordance with the truth and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir. When I gave information and declaration, I also did it to Kosova police and other bodies and I did that in order to shed light on crimes, in order to prevent crimes which are continuing to happen in Kosova. So in view of what I said earlier, I had today this opportunity to express my views today, and again I'm telling you that I do not accept what has happened and I cannot give testimony to -- on these things which have happened there; I cannot do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to invite the parties to assist the Chamber in making a determination specifically in respect of the application of Rule 77. I leave to the parties who would like to speak first. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I wonder if it might be sensible at this point to adjourn the proceedings as far as the witness is concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the witness is then ordered to remain stand-by.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And for the parties to have an opportunity to collect their thoughts and perhaps to have inter partes discussions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- for ten minutes or so and then for the Bench to re-convene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kabashi, you are ordered to remain stand-by, you'll follow the usher. You should remain in this building and the Chamber will consider what should be done and the Chamber in your absence will first hear from the parties what they suggest that should be done under the present circumstances. We stand adjourned for 15 minutes until quarter to 12.00. --- Break taken at 11.28 a.m. ORIE: Yes. Mr. Kabashi, you are ordered to stand-by, follow the usher, to remain in this building and then the Chamber will consider what should be done and will hear from the parties what should be done in the present circumstances. We stand adjourned for 15 minutes until quarter to 12.00. --- Break taken at 11.28 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've asked that the witness be kept out of court for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that, as a matter of fact, is what the Chamber had in mind as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I indicate that the discussions that have been had at the bar have identified really three broad categories of issue which arise I think in the following sequential order: Number one, have we reached a position already, this witness having expressed the view I think now on eight separate occasions that he's not prepared to testify, that the matter has been taken as far with the witness as it is proper to take it. That is the first question, as we submit. The second question if there is to be consideration given to contempt for proceedings, is it appropriate for this Trial Chamber to be the Trial Chamber that exercises the decision-making powers vested under Rule 77 or should it be another Trial Chamber. And thirdly, what steps, if any, does the Trial Chamber have lawfully to deprive this individual of his liberty pending any determination that there may be as to what steps should be taken in relation to him, that not being the power that's provided either under the Statute or the Rules. Can I deal with the first point first, because really that is the crucial question, has the matter been taken as far as it ought to be taken at this stage. I think on this there is something of a difference of opinion between Prosecution and Defence. The view of the Defence is that the witness has now made his position clear on eight separate occasions in the course of the testimony that he's given. Whether that amounts to a refusal or a refusal with excuses is a matter not, we would submit, for exploration by this Trial Chamber at this point because it is clear that the witness is not willing to testify. I understand that the Prosecution has a different proposal and there are in essence two prongs to it. The first prong is that the witness should be given another opportunity to see whether he is willing to testify, and put in those terms alone and providing the questions were put by the Bench, that is not a course that I would necessarily oppose. But the second prong to the Prosecution's suggestion is that, in fact, they should ignore, in effect, the expressed wishes of the witness and proceed to attempt to examine him, and in so doing, to put to him his witness statement and invite him to confirm that its contents are true, and then in effect tender him for cross-examination. I'm going to let them elaborate that proposal fairly and openly. I've indicated to them that if that is their proposal, they should seek a ruling from the Trial Chamber before doing so because that is a proposal which we would most firmly oppose. It would be quite, in our submission, improper for the Prosecution to seek to obtain 92 ter confirmation of evidence in chief, knowing that a witness is not prepared to give evidence on oath in support of the substance of the evidence in chief or make himself available properly for cross-examination upon it. The Trial Chamber has already ruled that where 92 ter material is to be elicited, it should at least briefly be elicited orally in substance and there's a reason for that. I appreciate that these circumstances have arisen rather shortly of that ruling and may appear on their face to be exceptional. But the underlying reason for it is we cannot have, in our respectful submission, a fair trial taking place where, knowing that a witness has adopted the posture that this witness has adopted, the Prosecution seeks in effect to obviate the need for evidence in chief by slipping through the witness an affirmation of the content, either of the evidence that he gave on oath in Limaj or the evidence that's represented in the various witness statements. The statements differ one from another in content at various points. The evidence in Limaj differs in certain respects from the evidence in the statements. To ask a witness whether what he said on oath in a previous trial was the truth or a lie is to invite an admission of perjury. And the situation is absolutely full of minefield difficulties, but above all it's an improper, in our submission, use of the prosecutorial function. And so if this witness is to be given another opportunity to re-consider his position, then in our submission that should be confined to asking him the question, yes or no, have you changed your mind. It should be a question put from the Bench and he should be given an opportunity to answer it. No further questioning should take place as to his motives or reasons. If they are to be explored they may have to be explored with the benefit of counsel and after caution perhaps by another Trial Chamber. But all that can properly be done, in our submission, at this stage is for this Trial Chamber to ask the witness whether he has reconsidered or whether he wishes further time to consider his position but not to embark on what purports to be and enforced examination-in-chief, but really in the full knowledge of the Prosecution, he's only going to go as far as trying to get a confirmation of previous testimony and then sitting down and claiming that that's evidence in chief. That's our submission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, Mr. Harvey, anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, would you like to make any submissions on the matter, apart from -- I take it that you also understood that Mr. Emmerson eloquently told us that this is a minefield. The Chamber is aware of the mines it has detected. If there are any other mines, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll give him eloquence but not actually accuracy in terms of what my submissions were going to be on this point. The Prosecution's submissions on the point are that it has not yet reached the point under Rule 77 or dealing with the witness in relation to possible contempt. The witness, we have all heard, has expressed some reluctance to testify. Our submission is the following procedure should occur. The witness should be brought back into court and the Prosecution should be allowed to continue to see whether the witness is prepared to go further. We have only gone so far in terms of the testimony we have sought to elicit from him. The first thing we'd do would be to go back to the Rule 92 ter intended statement. He's already said on the record that it's correct. We would then take it to him and continue in the normal process of giving evidence. In effect what I'm saying is that the witness should be given another chance. The Prosecution is anxious not to have witnesses dealt with under Rule 77 if it can possibly be avoided, and we are of the view it is not yet at that point. So the witness should be brought back and given the chance. Now, what happens after that if the witness is reluctant or does not wish or expresses a refusal to testify in the face of the Tribunal is a matter which should be pursued by the Trial Chamber. And the other issues to which Mr. Emmerson has alluded are matters slightly further down the track. Prosecution is not intending just to bring the witness in and say, Is this your statement, is it correct, and sit down. That would be, in my submission, a misuse of Rule 92 ter and we certainly would not be intending to do that at all. We would intend to see whether the witness is prepared to testify and see how far we can -- we can go. Another suggestion was made during discussions between counsel inter partes, which was if the witness still refuses to testify or expresses reluctance, that he could be granted a further "cooling-off period," as indeed was the case adopted by the Trial Chamber in the Bulatovic contempt issue in the Milosevic case in which the witness was basically sent home - I'm sorry - sent away overnight and asked to come back the next day to see whether he would reconsider. Those -- that would be the preferred course of course -- preferred course of action from the Prosecution, and it is only once you reach that stage that further action should be taken. But we also note - and this is quite important - that the 92 ter statement was signed on Friday, the 1st of June, and the Prosecution actually provided the statement to the witness in his own language on May the 16th. So the witness has had the statement in his own language and in English for two weeks before he came to The Hague and has had that statement, a signed copy of the statement since last Friday, and it's now Tuesday. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I respond briefly? First of all, the witness has given two answers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give you an opportunity, just to know for sure, the 92 ter statement is the short statement signed on the 1st of June, I take it, Mr. Re, that is, in which at least quite a lot of details in ill-treatment in Jablanica were left out?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Only because those were the parts we intended to lead orally from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, just for my --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- understanding that there's no confusion about that. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There is quite a lot of material in that which also appears in the consolidated witness statement and which would have been the subject of evidence in chief, and so to that extent there's material in that statement that goes directly to the alleged responsibility of the accused, but Your Honour's quite right that some of the key aspects of the evidence are not contained within it. This witness has given conflicting answers in respect of -- and indeed to some respect opaque answers in respect of the correctness of what was recorded. His first response was to say to Your Honour that the statement had not been properly considered by him and he had not had an opportunity to assimilate the detail. Whether that is true or not, according to what the Prosecution says, that was his first answer. He later gave an answer which was not specific to any particular witness statement, but was to previous accounts given, which was in answer to the question put by Your Honour in relation to whether his concern was that he'd previously lied on oath, for example, which is with respect a difficult question to put to a witness whilst on oath during the course of a trial; in any event, it represents its own potential minefield. The way that Mr. Re puts it, I'm glad to hear involves a recognition that it would be a misuse by the Prosecution of Rule 92 ter to proceed to put to the witness the witness's statement and at that stage, in full recognition of the fact he wasn't prepared to testify orally, to seek to rely on that. That at least is some firm ground beneath the parties' feet, because that's not the way, with the greatest of respect, the matter was outlined to me in the break but it perhaps involves a misunderstanding by me of what I was being told. That's why I insisted that the matter be brought to the Trial Chamber for a ruling. It seems to me, with respect, that if what Mr. Re is really trying to find out is whether this witness is genuinely willing to testify orally and that is really what the Prosecution seeks to do, then that is a matter that can best be achieved by the Trial Chamber asking him if he has changed his mind and, if not, whether a further period of reflection overnight might assist him to change his mind. Those are questions to which I would not object. If Your Honour is against me - and I must say I do urge most strongly that that be as far as it be taken at this stage and see how the witness responds, because that is a genuine inquiry to see if he is willing to testify orally. If Your Honour is against me as an alternative position that the Prosecution should in our submission as a minimum be required and confined to examining the substance of his testimony orally. If what Mr. Re says is right and the Prosecution is not seeking through the proposed course of action to obviate the problem by getting agreement to a 92 ter statement and then in full knowledge that the witness won't give oral testimony rely upon that, then the right and proper course would be to put the 92 ter statement only at the very end in re-examination once he's given oral evidence of the substance, but not, as is obviously the risk - and indeed, Mr. Re acknowledges this - to move within three questions to say, is this your statement, did you tell the truth or did you lie, were you committing perjury when you gave evidence in Limaj, and at that point the witness says, I'm not prepared to answer any further questions and we find ourselves in a situation which is entirely predictable as we stand here now. So two submissions: First of all, the right course, and really the only right course now, is for the Trial Chamber to take responsibility for asking the questions of the witness, not the Prosecution and for them to ask the question, have you changed your mind; if not, would further time assist you? If Your Honour is against me, then I've made the alternative submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, any need to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Prosecution doesn't agree in the -- with the way it's been expressed by Mr. Emmerson in a sense that it is a black and white situation of what he said in Limaj contradicts what he says in his statement, therefore there's a question of perjury. The Prosecution is of the view that it's far more nuanced and there are ways which things people say -- any differences can be reconciled and can be done on the record. The Prosecution's proposal is that it continue with the questioning to see whether the witness will testify and how far he would go. All I was saying is, we would not say, Is this your statement, 92 bis, and then sit down; we would wish to take it further. So those are the submissions as to how we would deal with the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will proceed mainly in accordance with the line suggested by Mr. Emmerson, and the Chamber would like to ask Madam Usher to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, the Chamber has observed that you repeatedly told us that you would not answer questions put to you by the parties or by the Bench. The Chamber also carefully listened to the reasons you have presented for not answering questions. The reasons you've given have not convinced the Chamber that these are reasons justifying a refusal to answer questions where you are here as a witness. The Chamber, therefore, would like to remind you of your duty; that is, to testify and answer questions. Now, since you left the courtroom, almost one hour passed. And I take it that you have given it some thought, the present situation, as the Chamber and the parties have given it some thought how to proceed. May I first ask you: Do you still insist, that is, that you'll not answer questions put to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I heard you through interpretation. You said that I do not accept answering the questions and do not want to answer questions. I have never said this. I have never said I do not want, that I refuse. I have never said this so far. I have said that I cannot. If you understand me, I -- it's not possible for me to respond to questions and continue to respond questions about the events. I've never said I refuse and that I do not want. If you want clarifications or if you want some cases from me, I could give you, but I've never said that I do not want and I reject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, let's be quite clear. To testify means to answer the questions put to you by those who are examining you; that is, if you fail to answer a question -- now, quite simply, if Ms. Issa, and later Defence counsel and the Bench, would put questions to you, would you answer them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said earlier, it is not that I do not want to answer questions; however, on basis of the cases that have occurred and the circumstances in the country I live, which is most important --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't want -- I don't want any further explanation at this moment. I just want to know if I invite Ms. Issa to continue the examination, will you answer her questions, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have wished to, but I cannot. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that you will not respond to her questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, your answers are not unambiguous. Therefore, we'll find out what happens. I'll give an opportunity to Ms. Issa to continue the examination. Ms. Issa, at the same time, you are -- you are guided just to put questions to the witness and not to start with seeking confirmation of a written statement. I'm not saying that this should be excluded, but that's not the starting point for your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I indicate in that connection I have a standing objection to that course, and the moment any thought is given by the Prosecution to pursuing it, I would like a ruling from the Trial Chamber after argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I similarly would have a standing objection. I also believe that -- at least as I understand English, and I don't know whether or not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a -- Mr. Guy-Smith --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- the issue between "cannot" and "will not" is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- is where I think, if there would be an ambiguity, that would be the ambiguity that would have been articulated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, the proof of the pudding is in this case in the eating and we'll -- with all the caution I gave, we'll try to find out what, just by experiencing, what the position of the witness is. Ms. Issa, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, drawing your attention to the year 1998. Were you a member of the KLA at that point?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Gentlemen, I apologise, I cannot to talk about these things. [In English] I'm done. I cannot do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, you're invited -- the question was quite simple. Your attention was drawn to 1998. The question was whether you were a member of the KLA at that point in time. If 1998 is too vague for you, if you would like to have that specified, please ask further specification; if not, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, Your Honour, I believe that in my estimation - and I understand the Chamber has perhaps a different view - he has answered the question. I also am concerned by virtue of my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I now want to proceed as I indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The reason I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi -- Mr. Guy-Smith --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The reason I'm imposing is because an issue of potential -- there's a legal issue that exists with an issue of potential waiver in the event that there are further legal proceedings that may occur with this young man, and he cannot be put in a position where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- Where his testimony would allow him to be put in a legal compromised position of having waived --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- Any legal rights that he might have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Guy-Smith, it's clear. Mr. Kabashi, if you would have any hesitation to answer this question because you at any earlier occasion would have not told the truth about the matter, then please tell us. We could try to find a solution for that problem. But if you answer the question now, it should be in full accordance with the truth. Could you answer the question about whether you were a KLA member in 1998 or at any moment in 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said, sir, I'm not hesitant, it's not a matter of hesitation. I mentioned some earlier cases. There are many others which have to do with these things. It is not that I hesitate, but I cannot and I cannot. I cannot go through this trial -- with this question. I am not in a position. I cannot do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Issa, the Chamber considers this a failure to answer a question, and in view of the approach taken by the witness until now, the Chamber considers it not very useful that you continue your examination-in-chief at this moment. We'll go a different direction now. Mr. Kabashi, as I said before, you told us what your position was in relation to giving testimony in this court. You gave some reasons. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You gave the reasons for this approach -- I would now like to finish, Mr. Emmerson. You gave the reasons. I reminded you of your duties in this respect. The Chamber established a couple of seconds ago that you failed to answer a question. The Chamber, therefore, finds that you have not changed your mind, compared to the position you took approximately one hour ago. Before we continue, I would like to inform you that in the present circumstances the Chamber considers it necessary to provide legal counsel to you, because the Chamber considers that you should not do without it at this moment. For that very reason, Madam Usher, could you please ask Mr. Karnavas, who is waiting outside of this courtroom, to enter the courtroom. Mr. Karnavas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar asked which side I would have to put you. I answer to her "in the middle," Mr. Karnavas. Could you take a seat, and that seat is considered to be in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, we invited Mr. Karnavas to enter this courtroom. Mr. Karnavas is a -- is an experienced lawyer practising before this Tribunal. Mr. Karnavas, we invited you after we were informed that you would be willing to provide counsel to Mr. Kabashi, at least provisionally. I mean, we can't talk about eternity, but at least temporarily you were willing to provide counsel to Mr. Kabashi. Just for your information, the Chamber, it took us some time, we heard the submissions of the parties on how to proceed in the present circumstances, where Mr. Kabashi expressed - parties' views are different, reluctance, unwillingness, refusal, that's a matter of qualification - but at least he expressed that he would rather not testify. Since there was some ambiguity, the Chamber allowed the Prosecution to continue examination-in-chief, and Mr. Kabashi failed to answer the first question put to him by Ms. Issa. Under the present circumstances, the Chamber would like to explain to Mr. Kabashi what the procedure is that will follow. Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Karnavas is coming in at a rather late stage in the process, and I don't know whether it would in any way assist Your Honours to have some short submissions on what the next step in the process ought to be, because there seems to be very little in the Tribunal's jurisprudence on the interpretation and activation of Rule 77. I have in the course of the break e-mailed to the Trial Chamber a decision of the European Court of Human Rights about the appropriateness of one Tribunal dealing with a contempt committed before that Tribunal which contains some comparative jurisprudence and some fairly strong warning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll look at it. Mr. Emmerson, please be advised that just as you are working hard on the breaks, the Chamber does as well --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and that no final decisions at this moment are made but --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That was all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I'll explain to you what the Chamber -- just to inform the witness, what is a envisaged course to proceed. The Chamber, Mr. Kabashi, might decide to proceed under Rule 77. That means that the Chamber should believe that -- or at least that it has reasons to believe that you are in contempt if we would have reasons to believe that and that would then focus on contempt of court under Rule 77(A)(i), which reads that someone can be held in contempt: "being a witness before a Chamber, contumaciously refuses or fails to answer a question." We could also look at it in a broader way, that is, your -- what you said about your testimony in more general terms before this Tribunal. The Chamber has then several options. One of the options would be that the Chamber would invite the Prosecution to further investigate the matter and to bring an indictment against you; another option would be that the Chamber would prosecute the case itself, that's an issue on which Mr. Emmerson has -- has brought to our attention decisions of the European Court of Human Rights. So that's, I would say, a practical matter, that is, who should prosecute contempt of court. Then if this Chamber would do it itself, then we would consider when we would hear such a case, and if it is not this Chamber that would hear the contempt case, then of course we would have to consider when another Chamber would be available to hear a contempt case. Whatever the Chamber will decide, it should be clear to you that - and this is an order of the Chamber - you would have to keep yourself available. What we'll do at this moment is to adjourn for some 45 minutes. During these 45 minutes, Mr. Karnavas is available for you to consult. There will be an interpreter available. Once you've consulted Mr. Karnavas, the Chamber will have given it additional thought on how to proceed, of course depending on the situation that is in existence then, and then draft your options. We'll not -- I'll not anticipate on those options. But at this moment, you're ordered not to leave the premises of the Tribunal at this moment. Mr. Karnavas will certainly be able to explain to you what would be the consequences if you would leave the premises, and in addition to this, until matters have been resolved, you're also ordered not to leave the territory of the Netherlands. Mr. Karnavas also will be in a position to explain to you what it would mean if you would not follow this order. Is that clear to you, Mr. Kabashi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll adjourn until 20 minutes past 1.00, and then we'll resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, did you have an opportunity to consult with Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has he explained to you your present situation and also what the consequences may be if you persist in the position you've taken until now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Kabashi, before I ask you whether your position has changed, I have to warn you that the consequences I -- possible consequences I did put to you before the break might become reality; that is, that you might be prosecuted and sentenced, maximum penalty for contempt of court is a long term of imprisonment, maximum seven years. This is not to say that for contempt cases usually seven years are imposed, but I have to put to you how serious consequences can be. May I ask you, Mr. Kabashi, did you change your mind as -- yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- Mr. President, Your Honours, good morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. If I may, I did speak with the gentleman. I did go over all his rights and the consequences. He's very well aware of the consequences, and I've indicated to him that I would speak on his behalf if that would be okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And here is our respective position, Mr. President, Your Honours. At this point in time, as he's indicated in the past, not that he does not want to, but he believes that he is not in a position, he's unable psychologically and for other reasons, to answer any questions and doesn't wish to any questions and realises the consequences that may follow. But nonetheless, that is his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is, basically his position has not changed compared to the position he took before the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, I just wanted to seek your confirmation that what Mr. Karnavas just told us is your position - and I ask you this question taking it that you are fully aware of possible consequences. Could you confirm that what Mr. Karnavas just said is the position you take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir. This is my position. I tried to explain to you earlier about the injustices made during the investigations into the events that occurred to me about the situation I am in. If this is not sufficient, I do not have anything to add. I stand by what Mr. Karnavas has just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Kabashi, for that. The Chamber has considered what to do under the present circumstances, and the Chamber has decided that it would issue an order in lieu of an indictment under Rule 77, 77(D). Mr. Emmerson, you have drawn the attention of the Chamber to Cypriotic case before the European Court of Human Rights. If the Chamber remembers well, it's not the first time that you have drawn our attention to that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think it is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh. I remember that I saw you appearing at another occasion where --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's a different case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I remember two decisions but okay. We have studied that and the Chamber has looked at this decision, has noticed that there are two important features that distinguish the case dealt with by the European Court of Human Rights and the present case. The first one being that the Judges themselves were the object and target of the contemptuous expressions by the lawyer at that time. The second one is the way in which in that case the Chamber proceeded. If you can talk about summary proceedings, they were very summarious.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the Chamber considers the way it proceeds not to be similar to what it has done, so for those reasons were the Chamber will, apart from issuing an order, will also decide to prosecute the matter itself and the Chamber will do it in the following way --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I only pause because the purpose of bringing that decision to the Trial Chamber's attention was entirely recognising that the factual circumstances in that case were different, but nonetheless in the first part of the Article 6 decision and looking at what was considered to be comparative jurisprudence in support of that proposition, a strong presumption against a Trial Chamber dealing summarily with the contempt in the face of the Court, unless it was strictly necessary in order to enable the proceedings to continue. Now, it occurs to me - and I'm -- this is not even remotely to be taken as any kind of criticism at all because I think it is inevitable in exploring contempt in the course of proceedings, that a Judge may come to express certain opinions to the witness in the course of questioning them, which if I were representing the witness and in Mr. Karnavas's position may cause me to make submissions, not analogous directly to the Kyprianov case but on the first limb of Article 6 that there is an appearance, not an actual bias, but an appearance of the bias of having a Tribunal who appears to have expressed a view as to whether or not a person is in contempt then going on to try with the presumption of innocence whether they are not. And before Your Honours make a decision, I wondered whether Mr. Karnavas might -- it's really not my issue, although to some extent, since you are the Trial Chamber for my own accused as well, there is a cross-over. But I wonder whether Mr. Karnavas has had the opportunity to consider those passages in the transcript against the jurisprudence and to make submissions to Your Honours if he thinks it right, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and I thank Mr. Emmerson for bringing the case to my attention. I was familiar with it because I had read it in the past. I haven't studied the transcript as thoroughly as I would have liked to. I do take on point what Mr. Emmerson seems to be indicating. I think as a matter of caution it might be best to have the matter heard before another three Judges, but at this point in time I haven't heard what the Trial Chamber intends to do. I haven't -- I mean, you were stopped midway and so it might be a bit premature for me to sort of -- and I'm not clairvoyant, so I don't know exactly what you intend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the matter, Mr. Karnavas, and the Chamber -- well, to give you a glance at what you could expect, the Chamber is about to issue an order and to decide to prosecute the matter itself, which of course does not preclude you from raising any defence of the Chamber being biased or -- well, to follow whatever is under -- in the Cypriotic case is raised under Article 6 of the European Convention of Human Rights. So the mere fact that we order the Prosecution and that we decide that it will be this Chamber to prosecute itself, following the Bulatovic precedent, does not prevent you in any way from --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Might the Prosecution be very briefly heard on that point. In our view it's important that the Prosecution's submission is put before the Chamber or at least is on the record at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution views what has happened today as extremely serious. There would appear to an objective outsider to be an element of sabotage from the witness, a former KLA member, coming here and declaring he wasn't going to testify, having not -- and said on the record he had given no indication of this before. The Trial Chamber has a very serious and onerous task in trying to establish the truth, and it is important for public justice that all witnesses or all relevant evidence is heard. And such behaviour before the Trial Chamber, in the face of the Trial Chamber, should not be countenanced. And the Prosecution fully supports the Trial Chamber issuing an order that the witness be prosecuted for contempt.
